terms.sub: Gram Stain Mechanism and Cell Wall Architecture
clues: Composed of alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) chains cross-linked by transpeptidases.
Targeted directly by beta-lactam antibiotics, glycopeptides, and host lysozyme.
The rigid structural meshwork polymer that is thick in Gram-positive bacteria and thin in Gram-negative bacteria.

terms.sub: Gram Stain Mechanism and Cell Wall Architecture
clues: Consists of an outer O-antigen polysaccharide, a core oligosaccharide, and a toxic lipid A anchor.
Binds CD14 and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on macrophages to trigger septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
The heat-stable endotoxin found exclusively in the outer leaflet of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane.

terms.sub: Gram Stain Mechanism and Cell Wall Architecture
clues: Polymers of ribitol phosphate or glycerol phosphate found exclusively in Gram-positive envelopes.
Contributes to the net negative surface charge of Gram-positive cocci and bacilli and activates TLR2.
A cell wall polymer covalently linked to peptidoglycan or anchored to the plasma membrane in Gram-positive bacteria.
Exists in both a cell-wall-bound clumping factor form and a secreted extracellular form.
Binds human prothrombin to form staphylothrombin, converting fibrinogen into a protective fibrin coat.
The key diagnostic enzyme that distinguishes Staphylococcus aureus from Staphylococcus epidermidis.
Examples include staphylococcal TSST-1, staphylococcal enterotoxins, and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A.
Bypasses normal intracellular antigen processing by cross-linking MHC class II directly to the V-beta region of T-cell receptors.
A bacterial toxin that polyclonally activates up to 20% of host T cells, triggering a massive life-threatening cytokine storm.
Identified in the laboratory by optochin susceptibility, bile solubility, and a positive Quellung reaction.
Appears on Gram stain as lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci.
The leading bacterial cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia, adult meningitis, and otitis media.
Formed by members of the genera Bacillus and Clostridium during nutrient starvation.
Contains calcium dipicolinate in its core, conferring resistance to boiling, desiccation, and chemical disinfectants.
A dormant, highly resistant bacterial survival structure requiring autoclaving at 121 degrees Celsius for destruction.
Travels via retrograde axonal transport from peripheral wounds to the anterior horn of the spinal cord.
Cleaves synaptobrevin in Renshaw interneurons to block release of inhibitory GABA and glycine.
The potent neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani responsible for trismus (lockjaw) and generalized spastic paralysis.
Contains bile salts and crystal violet to inhibit the growth of Gram-positive organisms.
Incorporates lactose and neutral red pH indicator to differentiate pink lactose fermenters from colourless non-fermenters.
The standard selective and differential culture medium used to isolate and classify Enterobacteriaceae.
Binds to GM1 ganglioside receptors on small intestinal epithelial cells via its five B subunits.
Catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the Gs-alpha subunit, persistently activating adenylate cyclase.
The enterotoxin of Vibrio cholerae that elevates intracellular cAMP and causes profuse rice-water secretory diarrhoea.
Produces characteristic blue-green pyocyanin and fluorescent yellow-green pyoverdine pigments with a grape-like odour.
Causes malignant otitis externa, hot-tub folliculitis, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and ecthyma gangrenosum.
An opportunistic, oxidase-positive, strictly aerobic non-fermenting Gram-negative rod notorious for nosocomial multidrug resistance.
Prepared by gently heating sheep or horse blood agar to 80 degrees Celsius until erythrocytes lyse and turn brown.
Releases intracellular haemin (Factor X) and NAD (Factor V) while inactivating serum NADases.
An enriched non-selective culture medium required for primary isolation of Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria species.
